seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 101 HTS Chapter 25 lines — cement and clinker, salt, sulfur, gypsum, lime, sand, granite and marble blocks, graphite, barite, fluorspar and more. Base rates, the 2026 Section 301 rates and exemptions, China's 25–37.5%, and the antidumping order on Japanese cement.

overview.intro:
Chapter 25 covers salt, sulfur, earths and stone, plastering materials, lime and cement — the bulk minerals behind construction and industry: portland cement and clinker, road and table salt, gypsum, lime, sand and gravel, granite and marble blocks, and industrial minerals such as natural graphite, barite, fluorspar, magnesia, kaolin and talc. **91 of the 101 tariff lines are Free** under the general rate; the rest are cut stone, crude barite, calcined dolomite and micaceous iron oxides at 2.8–3% or $1.25/t. The U.S. imported **$6.06B** of these goods in 2025, $2.34B of it cement.

What decides the duty today is the country. The **2026 Section 301 tariffs** add 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies — Türkiye and Vietnam cement and Chilean salt pay 12.5% — but 19 subheadings of critical and industrial minerals (sulfur, natural graphite, phosphate rock, barite, magnesia, fluorspar and others) are on the exemption list in U.S. note 52(b). USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt, so most Canadian and Mexican cement, salt and gypsum enter Free. China pays 25% under List 3 plus 12.5% — 37.5% extra on most lines — and natural graphite from China 25% since January 1, 2026. Gray portland cement from Japan also carries an **antidumping duty**, which the tariff calculator does not include.

productGroups.label: Salt (road, rock, sea and table salt)
productGroups.blurb: Rock salt and road (deicing) salt, sea salt, table salt, brine and pure sodium chloride: one line, Free. Salt is not on any exemption list, so the 2026 Section 301 rates apply (Chile, Egypt and the Bahamas 12.5%); USMCA salt from Canada and Mexico is Free. Salt for food or feed needs an FDA prior notice.

productGroups.label: Unroasted iron pyrites
productGroups.blurb: Unroasted iron pyrites: one line, Free.

productGroups.label: Sulfur (crude and other)
productGroups.blurb: Crude or unrefined sulfur and other sulfur (granular, prilled, molten): 2 lines, Free and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)). China pays 25% (List 3) and Brazil 25%. Sublimed, precipitated and colloidal sulfur are in heading 2802.

productGroups.label: Natural graphite
productGroups.blurb: Natural flake, powder and other graphite: 3 lines, Free and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)). Natural graphite from China pays 25% under Section 301 since January 1, 2026 (9903.91.06). Synthetic (artificial) graphite is heading 3801.

productGroups.label: Natural sands (silica, quartz and other sand)
productGroups.blurb: Silica and quartz sand (including sand with 95% or more silica, used for glass and fracking) and other natural sands: 3 lines, Free. Metal-bearing sands are in chapter 26.

productGroups.label: Quartz and quartzite
productGroups.blurb: Quartz other than natural sand, and quartzite crude or cut into blocks or slabs: 4 lines, Free. Engineered quartz countertops and slabs are not here (heading 6810).

productGroups.label: Kaolin (china clay)
productGroups.blurb: Kaolin and other kaolinic clays, calcined or not: one line, Free. On Brazil's Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)), not on the 2026 list.

productGroups.label: Other clays (bentonite, ball clay, fire-clay)
productGroups.blurb: Bentonite, fire-clay, ball clay and other clays, fuller's earth, andalusite, kyanite, sillimanite, mullite and chamotte: 8 lines, Free. Expanded clays are heading 6806.

productGroups.label: Chalk
productGroups.blurb: Natural chalk, crude or other: 2 lines, Free. Writing, drawing and billiard chalks are not here (headings 9609 and 9504).

productGroups.label: Natural calcium phosphates (phosphate rock)
productGroups.blurb: Natural calcium phosphates and phosphatic chalk, unground or ground: 2 lines, Free and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) and Brazil's list. China pays 25% (List 3). Peru is the main supplier.

productGroups.label: Barite (barytes) and witherite
productGroups.blurb: Natural barium sulfate (barite) and barium carbonate (witherite): 3 lines. Ground barite is Free, crude barite $1.25/t (2511.10.50), witherite Free. Barite is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) and not on China's List 3, so it pays no extra tariff from most countries.

productGroups.label: Diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr)
productGroups.blurb: Siliceous fossil meals such as kieselguhr, tripolite and diatomite: one line, Free.

productGroups.label: Pumice, emery, corundum and garnet
productGroups.blurb: Pumice stone, emery, natural corundum, natural garnet and other natural abrasives: 4 lines, Free.

productGroups.label: Slate (blocks and slabs)
productGroups.blurb: Slate, crude or merely cut into blocks or slabs: one line, Free. Roofing and facing slates are heading 6803.

productGroups.label: Marble and travertine (blocks and slabs)
productGroups.blurb: Marble, travertine and other calcareous building stone, crude or merely cut into blocks or slabs: 4 lines. Crude and cut marble are Free; cut travertine and other calcareous stone pay 3%. Polished slabs and tiles are heading 6802.

productGroups.label: Granite, sandstone and other building stone
productGroups.blurb: Granite, porphyry, basalt, sandstone and other monumental or building stone, crude or merely cut into blocks or slabs: 7 lines. Crude stone is Free; cut granite pays 2.8% and cut sandstone and other stone 3%. Polished or worked stone, such as countertops, is heading 6802.

productGroups.label: Gravel, crushed stone and macadam
productGroups.blurb: Pebbles, gravel, crushed limestone and other stone for concrete aggregate, road and railway ballast, slag macadam, tarred macadam, and marble or granite granules and powder: 7 lines, Free. By note 3, goods that fit 2517 and another heading go here.

productGroups.label: Dolomite
productGroups.blurb: Dolomite, crude (Free) or calcined or sintered (3%): 2 lines. Dolomite ramming mix is heading 3816.

productGroups.label: Magnesite and magnesia
productGroups.blurb: Natural magnesium carbonate (magnesite), fused and dead-burned magnesia, caustic calcined magnesite and other magnesium oxide: 4 lines, Free. Three of them are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) and none is on China's List 3, so Chinese magnesia pays no extra tariff except the 'other' line (2519.90.50, 12.5%).

productGroups.label: Gypsum, anhydrite and plaster
productGroups.blurb: Natural gypsum and anhydrite, and plasters of calcined gypsum or calcium sulfate: 2 lines, Free. Gypsum board (drywall) is heading 6809.

productGroups.label: Limestone flux and limestone for lime or cement
productGroups.blurb: Limestone flux and limestone of a kind used to make lime or cement: one line, Free.

productGroups.label: Quicklime, slaked (hydrated) lime and hydraulic lime
productGroups.blurb: Quicklime, slaked (hydrated) lime and hydraulic lime: 3 lines, Free. Pure calcium oxide and hydroxide are heading 2825.

productGroups.label: Cement and cement clinker
productGroups.blurb: Portland cement (white and gray), aluminous cement, other hydraulic cements and cement clinker: 5 lines, Free. Cement is the largest import in the chapter. Gray portland cement and clinker from Japan are also under a 1991 antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Asbestos
productGroups.blurb: Crocidolite, amosite, chrysotile and other asbestos: 7 lines, Free. Chrysotile and amosite (2524.90) are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; crocidolite (2524.10) is not. EPA bans most chrysotile asbestos imports and requires notice for any other new use.

productGroups.label: Mica
productGroups.blurb: Crude mica, split block mica and splittings, mica powder and mica waste: 5 lines, Free. Crude mica (2525.10) is on Brazil's Section 301 exemption list. Worked and built-up mica are in chapter 68.

productGroups.label: Talc and steatite
productGroups.blurb: Natural steatite (soapstone) and talc, crushed or not: 2 lines, Free. Not on China's List 3, so Chinese talc pays only the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 rate.

productGroups.label: Natural borates
productGroups.blurb: Natural sodium and calcium borates and their concentrates (not borates separated from natural brine): 3 lines, Free. Refined borax and boric acid are chapter 28.

productGroups.label: Feldspar, nepheline syenite and fluorspar
productGroups.blurb: Feldspar, leucite, nepheline syenite and fluorspar (acid and metallurgical grade): 5 lines, Free. Fluorspar (2529.21, 2529.22) is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) and not on China's List 3, so no Section 301 duty applies to it from any country.

productGroups.label: Other minerals (vermiculite, perlite, Epsom salts, earth colors)
productGroups.blurb: Unexpanded vermiculite, perlite and chlorites, kieserite and natural Epsom salts, natural cryolite, micaceous iron oxides (2.9%), celestite, earth colors and other minerals: 8 lines. Most are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; vermiculite and perlite (2530.10) are not.

workedExamples.title: A cargo of portland cement from Türkiye
workedExamples.body: Gray portland cement is **Free** under the general rate, but it is not on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list, so goods of Türkiye pay the **12.5%** 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.79). On a $1,000,000 cargo that is **$125,000**. The same cement from Canada or Mexico is Free when entered under USMCA (9903.05.93 / 9903.05.94); from Vietnam or Egypt it is also 12.5%, from Greece or Spain 10% (the EU rate, 9903.05.39).

workedExamples.title: Road salt from Chile vs. Canada
workedExamples.body: Salt is Free under the general rate. Chilean salt pays the **12.5%** Section 301 duty on Chile (9903.05.30) even with a U.S.–Chile FTA claim, because note 52(a) keeps the duty for FTA goods: $600,000 of rock salt pays **$75,000**. Canadian salt entered under USMCA pays **$0**. Between August 22 and September 14, 2026, Canadian salt and portland cement paid an extra **50%** under Section 338 (9903.03.14), USMCA or not, until Proclamation 11065 took them off the list.

workedExamples.title: Natural flake graphite from China
workedExamples.body: Crystalline flake graphite is Free under the general rate and on the note 52(b) exemption list, so the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply. Since **January 1, 2026** Chinese natural graphite pays **25%** (9903.91.06, from the 2024 four-year review): $200,000 of flake pays **$50,000**. Flake from Mozambique, Madagascar or Brazil pays nothing extra. The ITC voted on April 3, 2026 not to impose antidumping or countervailing duties on active anode material from China, so no AD/CVD order applies.

workedExamples.title: Granite blocks cut into slabs, from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Granite merely cut into slabs at least 7.5 cm thick carries a **2.8%** base rate. Goods of Brazil add the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty (9903.05.01) and the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.27): **40.3%** in total, or $40,300 on $100,000. From India the same slabs pay 12.8% (2.8% + 10%); from Italy or Spain 10% (the EU rate replaces the 2.8%). Polished or edged slabs and countertops are classified in heading 6802, not here.

**Note 1.** Except where their context or note 4 to this chapter otherwise requires, the headings of this chapter cover only products which are in the crude state or which have been washed (even with chemical substances eliminating the impurities without changing the structure of the product), crushed, ground, powdered, levigated, sifted, screened, concentrated by flotation, magnetic separation or other mechanical or physical processes (except crystallization), but not products which have been roasted, calcined, obtained by mixing or subjected to processing beyond that mentioned in each heading. The products of this chapter may contain an added anti-dusting agent, provided that such addition does not render the product particularly suitable for a specific use rather than for general use.

**Note 2.** This chapter does not cover: (a) sublimed sulfur, precipitated sulfur or colloidal sulfur (heading 2802); (b) earth colors containing 70 percent or more by weight of combined iron evaluated as Fe2O3 (heading 2821); (c) medicaments or other products of chapter 30; (d) perfumery, cosmetic or toilet preparations (chapter 33); (e) dolomite ramming mix (heading 3816); (f) setts, curbstones or flagstones (heading 6801); mosaic cubes and the like (heading 6802); roofing, facing or damp course slates (heading 6803); (g) precious or semiprecious stones (heading 7102 or 7103); (h) cultured crystals (other than optical elements) weighing not less than 2.5 g each, of sodium chloride or of magnesium oxide, of heading 3824; optical elements of sodium chloride or of magnesium oxide (heading 9001); (ij) billiard chalks (heading 9504); or (k) writing or drawing chalks or tailors' chalks (heading 9609).

**Note 3.** Any products classifiable in heading 2517 and any other heading of the chapter are to be classified in heading 2517.

**Note 4.** Heading 2530 applies, inter alia, to: vermiculite, perlite and chlorites, unexpanded; earth colors, whether or not calcined or mixed together; natural micaceous iron oxides; meerschaum (whether or not in polished pieces); amber; agglomerated meerschaum and agglomerated amber, in plates, rods, sticks or similar forms, not worked after molding; jet; strontianite (whether or not calcined), other than strontium oxide; broken pieces of pottery, brick or concrete.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 25: Salt, Sulfur, Earths & Stone, Lime and Cement — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 25 Tariff Updates — Cement, Salt, Graphite & Stone Tariffs Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for cement, salt, sulfur, gypsum, stone and graphite imports since January 2025: the IEEPA duties and their end, the 2026 Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and their mineral exemptions, the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian salt and cement and its reversal, and China's graphite tariff — with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). The base rates of all 101 Chapter 25 lines are the same in both.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025, non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico paid IEEPA duties and goods of most other countries the reciprocal tariff (10%, later higher by country) — except 18 mineral subheadings such as graphite, barite, magnesia and fluorspar. Those duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that followed ran until July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** apply 10% or 12.5% to goods of 60 economies, with 19 Chapter 25 subheadings exempt (U.S. note 52(b)) and USMCA goods exempt. Canadian salt and cement also paid a **50% Section 338** duty from August 22 to September 14, 2026. China pays its 2018–2019 List 3 duty on top, and natural graphite from China pays 25% since January 1, 2026.

The antidumping order on **gray portland cement and clinker from Japan** is listed below for reference; antidumping duties are set by the Commerce Department and are **not included in the tariff calculator**.

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 25 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 101 Chapter 25 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no exemption list for Chapter 25. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect during the statutory review. The 25% List 3 duty on Chinese salt, cement, stone and other Chapter 25 goods continues.

changes.title: Section 338 duty on Canadian salt and cement removed
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 took salt (2501.00.00) and other portland cement (2523.29.00) off the 9903.03.14 list for goods entered from September 15, 2026, along with other subheadings. Since then Canadian salt and cement pay only the 2026 Section 301 rate (10%, or nothing with a USMCA claim).

changes.title: 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian salt and cement
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 (signed July 20, 2026) imposed a 50% duty under section 338 of the Tariff Act on listed products of Canada (9903.03.14, U.S. note 51(b)(3)), including salt (2501.00.00) and other portland cement (2523.29.00). Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026. The duty applied even to goods entered under USMCA (note 51(a)).

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies take effect
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on top of the base rate, including Türkiye, Vietnam, Chile, Egypt, Peru, India, the EU (10% in total) and non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico. 19 Chapter 25 subheadings are exempt under U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86); the other 74 lines are covered.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026; the 2026 Section 301 tariffs took over the next day.

changes.title: 25% Section 301 tariff on Brazil takes effect
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), on top of the base rate and the 12.5% 2026 duty. 20 Chapter 25 subheadings are exempt under U.S. note 50(a)(ii) (9903.05.03), including graphite, phosphate rock, barite, kaolin, crude mica and fluorspar; granite and other stone are covered.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply — and still lift the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican goods.

changes.title: No antidumping or countervailing duties on graphite anode material from China
changes.detail: Commerce found dumping and subsidies on active anode material from China (final determinations of February 17, 2026), but the ITC determined that the U.S. industry was not materially retarded, so no orders were issued. The investigation covered goods of 2504.10.10 and 2504.10.50 (natural graphite) as well as 3801.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico were exempt, and so were the same 18 mineral subheadings as under the reciprocal tariff (9903.03.03); sulfur, salt, cement, gypsum and stone paid.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24.

changes.title: Section 232 on processed critical minerals: negotiations, no tariff
changes.detail: Proclamation 11001 agreed with Commerce that imports of processed critical minerals and derivative products threaten national security, but directed Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements (including possible price floors) instead of imposing tariffs. No Section 232 duty applies to graphite, fluorspar, barite or other Chapter 25 minerals.

changes.title: 25% Section 301 tariff on natural graphite from China
changes.detail: As announced in the 2024 four-year review, natural graphite of China (2504.10.10, 2504.10.50, 2504.90.00) pays 25% from January 1, 2026 (9903.91.06, U.S. note 31(g)); before that it was not covered by the China Section 301 lists.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff raised to country-specific rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025 — for example 15% for Türkiye, 20% for Vietnam and 15% in total for the EU. The 18 exempt mineral subheadings stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% IEEPA duty on goods of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on goods of Brazil, on top of the reciprocal tariff, for goods entered from August 6, 2025; Brazilian granite and other stone paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada IEEPA duty raised to 35% on non-USMCA goods
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on Canadian goods not entered under USMCA from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on most Chapter 25 goods
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. 18 Chapter 25 subheadings — natural graphite, phosphate rock, barite, magnesite and magnesia (except 2519.90.50), chrysotile and amosite asbestos, fluorspar and the minerals of 2530.20 and 2530.90 — are on the exemption list printed in the schedule (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a)); cement, salt, sulfur, gypsum, lime and stone paid. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico, so USMCA-qualifying cement, salt and gypsum entered Free again. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, including Chapter 25 goods such as cement and salt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: EPA bans most chrysotile asbestos imports
changes.detail: EPA's TSCA rule prohibits importing chrysotile asbestos for chlor-alkali diaphragms after May 28, 2024 and for sheet gaskets after May 27, 2026, with limited phase-outs (40 CFR part 751, subpart I). This is an import ban, not a tariff.

changes.title: Antidumping order on cement and clinker from Japan continued
changes.detail: After the fifth five-year review, Commerce continued the 1991 antidumping order on gray portland cement and cement clinker from Japan (2523.29, 2523.10 and, when entered there, 2523.90). Commerce found that dumping margins of up to 69.89% would be likely if the order were revoked. Microfine cement is excluded. Not included in the tariff calculator.

changes.title: 35% in lieu of column 2 on certain Russian goods
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set a 35% rate in place of the column 2 rate for listed products of Russia (9903.90.08, U.S. note 30), including salt (2501), diatomite (2512), slate (2514), 'other' magnesia (2519.90.50) and 2530.90.80. Still in force.

changes.title: Antidumping order on Mexican cement revoked
changes.detail: Commerce revoked the antidumping order on gray portland cement and clinker from Mexico after the 2006 U.S.–Mexico cement agreement, so Mexican cement carries no antidumping duty.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 25 goods were **$6.06B in 2025**, +3.3% from $5.86B in 2024 and below the 2022 peak of $6.64B. **Cement** is the biggest item: $2.34B (39%), mostly gray portland cement ($1.85B) plus white cement ($207M) and clinker ($84M). It comes from **Türkiye** ($680M), **Canada** ($525M), **Vietnam** ($374M), Mexico ($140M), Egypt ($100M) and Greece ($98M).

**Salt** imports rose to $812M (+36% on $598M), led by Chile ($194M) and Canada ($159M), then Spain, Egypt, Mexico and the Bahamas. **Sulfur** jumped to $336M from $124M, $281M of it from Canada. Peru ships phosphate rock ($368M), China mainly magnesia ($147M) and natural graphite ($49M), India, Vietnam and Morocco barite, and Mexico and Canada fluorspar, feldspar and nepheline syenite (heading 2529).

Canada is the largest supplier overall ($1.64B, 27%), shipping cement, sulfur, crushed stone and salt that mostly enter Free under USMCA. The 2025 figures predate the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, which now add 10–12.5% on Turkish, Vietnamese, Egyptian and Chilean cement and salt but exempt the critical and industrial minerals. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Most Chapter 25 base rates are Free, so the total is mainly the **2026 Section 301 rate** of the country: 10% or 12.5%, or 10% in total for EU goods.

Two things change the answer. A **USMCA claim** removes the 10% duty on Canadian and Mexican goods — compare the two Canada and Mexico columns. And 19 mineral subheadings (sulfur, natural graphite, phosphate rock, barite, most magnesia, fluorspar and others) are **exempt** under U.S. note 52(b), so they stay Free from almost every country. China pays its List 3 duty on top (up to 37.5%), Brazil a further 25%. The table does **not** include the antidumping duty on cement from Japan.

seo.title: Importing Cement, Salt, Stone & Minerals: Required Documents and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 25) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 25 line — TSCA import certification, the EPA asbestos ban, FDA prior notice for food salt, USDA APHIS rules for clay, stone and soil, DOT hazmat for sulfur and asbestos, the antidumping order on Japanese cement — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, exempt subheadings, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 25 goods are Free under the general rate, so the levers that matter are about the **extra duties**: a USMCA claim removes the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican goods, the 19 exempt mineral subheadings pay no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country, and drawback can return duties on goods that are exported again. Gray portland cement from Japan carries an **antidumping duty** that the tariff calculator does not include.

The paperwork depends on the product: every bulk mineral needs a TSCA certification, asbestos is largely banned, salt for food needs an FDA prior notice, earth and stone must be free of soil, and sulfur and asbestos are hazardous materials in transport. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Compare countries of origin
levers.saves: Up to 12.5 points of duty: Türkiye, Vietnam, Egypt and Chile pay 12.5%, the EU and India 10%, USMCA goods and countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies nothing; China up to 37.5%

levers.caveat: Section 301 duties follow the country of origin, not the shipping country. Antidumping orders follow their own scope: cement ground in a third country from Japanese clinker may still be covered.

levers.caveat: Cement inside the scope pays the cash deposit set by Commerce even if entered under another HTS line.

rules.title: Minerals and chemical substances in bulk: TSCA import certification (positive or negative) at entry
Salt for food or animal feed: prior notice to FDA before the shipment arrives (2 to 8 hours ahead, by mode)
Clay, talc, chalk, slate, gravel, stone and quarry products: not 'soil' if free of organic material, so no APHIS permit, but inspected at the port; soil itself needs a permit
Sulfur or diatomaceous earth imported as a pesticide product: EPA Notice of Arrival before the shipment arrives

Sulfur (UN1350; molten UN2448, class 4.1), asbestos (UN2212, UN2590, class 9) and quicklime (UN1910, air only) are in the Hazardous Materials Table: check whether the shipment needs hazmat shipping papers, marking and packaging

Chrysotile asbestos: import banned for chlor-alkali diaphragms (after May 28, 2024) and sheet gaskets (after May 27, 2026), other uses phased out; any other new use of asbestos needs 90-day notice to EPA
Gray portland cement and clinker from Japan: antidumping duty cash deposit (not in the tariff calculator)

groups.label: Salt (road, rock, sea and table salt)
groups.note: Salt for human food or animal feed needs an FDA prior notice; road and industrial salt does not. Not on the Section 301 exemption list: USMCA salt is Free, Chilean salt pays 12.5%.

groups.label: Unroasted iron pyrites
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification.

groups.label: Sulfur (crude and other)
groups.note: Sulfur is a hazardous material in transport (check special provision 30 for formed sulfur such as prills and granules). Sulfur sold as a fungicide or other pesticide needs an EPA Notice of Arrival.

groups.label: Natural graphite
groups.note: No AD/CVD order: the ITC voted on April 3, 2026 against duties on active anode material from China. No Section 232 duty: Proclamation 11001 chose negotiations for critical minerals.

groups.label: Natural sands (silica, quartz and other sand)
groups.note: Sand must be free of soil and organic material; clean mineral sand needs no APHIS permit but can be inspected.

groups.label: Quartz and quartzite
groups.note: Quartz and quartzite must be free of soil. Engineered quartz slabs are heading 6810 and fall under other trade remedies.

groups.label: Kaolin (china clay)
groups.note: Kaolin and other clays are not 'soil' under APHIS rules if free of organic material.

groups.label: Other clays (bentonite, ball clay, fire-clay)
groups.note: Bentonite and other clays are not 'soil' under APHIS rules if free of organic material.

groups.label: Chalk
groups.note: Chalk is not 'soil' under APHIS rules if free of organic material.

groups.label: Natural calcium phosphates (phosphate rock)
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification. No AD/CVD order covers phosphate rock (the phosphate orders cover fertilizers of chapter 31).

groups.label: Barite (barytes) and witherite
groups.note: No AD/CVD order covers barite.

groups.label: Diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr)
groups.note: Diatomaceous earth sold as an insecticide is a pesticide product and needs an EPA Notice of Arrival.

groups.label: Pumice, emery, corundum and garnet
groups.note: Pumice and natural abrasives must be free of soil.

groups.label: Slate (blocks and slabs)
groups.note: Slate must be free of soil.

groups.label: Marble and travertine (blocks and slabs)
groups.note: Stone blocks and slabs must be free of soil. Polished or worked slabs and tiles are heading 6802.

groups.label: Granite, sandstone and other building stone
groups.note: Stone blocks and slabs must be free of soil. Polished granite and countertops are heading 6802.

groups.label: Gravel, crushed stone and macadam
groups.note: Gravel and crushed stone must be free of soil and organic material.

groups.label: Dolomite
groups.note: Dolomite must be free of soil.

groups.label: Magnesite and magnesia
groups.note: No AD/CVD order covers magnesia (the order on magnesia carbon bricks from China covers bricks, not raw magnesia).

groups.label: Gypsum, anhydrite and plaster
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification.

groups.label: Limestone flux and limestone for lime or cement
groups.note: Limestone must be free of soil.

groups.label: Quicklime, slaked (hydrated) lime and hydraulic lime
groups.note: Quicklime is a hazardous material only when shipped by air.

groups.label: Cement and cement clinker
groups.note: Gray portland cement and clinker from Japan are under an antidumping order; Mexican cement has not been since 2009.

groups.label: Asbestos
groups.note: Chrysotile asbestos imports are largely banned under TSCA; any other new use of asbestos needs EPA notice. Asbestos is a hazardous material in transport.

groups.label: Mica
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification.

groups.label: Talc and steatite
groups.note: Talc and steatite are not 'soil' under APHIS rules if free of organic material.

groups.label: Natural borates
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification.

groups.label: Feldspar, nepheline syenite and fluorspar
groups.note: No AD/CVD order covers fluorspar or feldspar.

groups.label: Other minerals (vermiculite, perlite, Epsom salts, earth colors)
groups.note: No agency rule beyond the TSCA certification.

seo.title: Cement, Salt & Stone Tariffs FAQ: Canada Cement, Graphite, Granite, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 25) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about Chapter 25 tariffs: is there a tariff on cement or salt, the Canadian cement tariff and its reversal, graphite tariffs on China, granite and marble tariffs, where the U.S. gets its cement and salt, and HS codes for cement, salt, gypsum, sand, graphite and sulfur.
keywords: is there a tariff on cement
is there a tariff on salt
where does the us import cement from
where does the us get salt from

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on cement, salt, stone and industrial minerals — by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: 91 of the 101 Chapter 25 lines are Free under the general rate; the extra cost comes from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs: 12.5% on cement and salt from Türkiye, Vietnam, Egypt and Chile, 10% in total for EU goods, nothing for USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico.

19 mineral subheadings — sulfur, natural graphite, phosphate rock, barite, most magnesia, fluorspar and others — are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. China still pays 25% on graphite and up to 37.5% on most other Chapter 25 goods.

The IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026, the Section 122 surcharge July 23, 2026, and the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian salt and cement lasted only from August 22 to September 14, 2026. Cement from Japan still carries an antidumping duty, not shown in the calculator.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cement?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on cement
faqs.answer: Cement (2523) is Free under the general rate, but since July 24, 2026 the 2026 Section 301 tariffs add 12.5% on cement from Türkiye, Vietnam, Egypt, Colombia and Algeria, 10% in total on EU cement (Greece, Spain, France) and 12.5% on Korean cement. Canadian and Mexican cement entered under USMCA pays nothing; Chinese cement pays 37.5%. Gray portland cement and clinker from Japan also pay an antidumping duty.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Canadian cement? What was the cement tariff reversal?
searchedAs: does the us import cement from canada
faqs.answer: Canadian cement entered under USMCA is Free; without a USMCA claim it pays the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty. From August 22 to September 14, 2026, Proclamation 11048 put a 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian portland cement (2523.29.00) and salt, even under USMCA; Proclamation 11065 removed both from the list for goods entered from September 15, 2026. Canada shipped $525M of cement to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import cement from?
searchedAs: where does the us import cement from
where does the us get its cement
how much cement does the us import
faqs.answer: The U.S. imported $2.34B of cement and clinker in 2025. The largest suppliers were Türkiye ($680M), Canada ($525M), Vietnam ($374M), Mexico ($140M), Egypt ($100M) and Greece ($98M). Most of it is gray portland cement (2523.29).

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on salt?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on salt
faqs.answer: Salt (2501.00.00), including road and rock salt, is Free under the general rate but not on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so salt from Chile, Egypt and the Bahamas pays 12.5%, EU salt 10% in total, and non-USMCA salt from Canada or Mexico 10%. USMCA salt is Free. Chinese salt pays 37.5%; Russian salt 47.5%. Canadian salt also paid a 50% Section 338 duty from August 22 to September 14, 2026.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. get its salt from?
searchedAs: where does the us get salt from
where does the us get road salt
where does the us get rock salt from
where does the us get most of its salt
faqs.answer: Salt imports were $812M in 2025 (+36% on 2024). Chile ($194M) and Canada ($159M) were the largest suppliers, followed by Spain ($77M), Egypt ($74M), Mexico ($70M) and the Bahamas ($27M).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for salt, sea salt or Epsom salt?
faqs.answer: All salt — table salt, sea salt, rock salt, road salt, brine and pure sodium chloride — is one line, 2501.00.00.00, Free. Natural Epsom salts are 2530.20.20 (Free), while chemically produced magnesium sulfate is in chapter 28 (2833.21). Salt tablets and seasoned salts are classified elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for cement?
searchedAs: hs code for white portland cement
faqs.answer: Heading 2523: cement clinker 2523.10, white portland cement 2523.21, other (gray, ordinary) portland cement 2523.29, aluminous cement 2523.30 and other hydraulic cements such as slag cement 2523.90. All are Free under the general rate. Cement board and concrete blocks are chapter 68, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for gypsum?
faqs.answer: Natural gypsum and anhydrite are 2520.10.00; plasters of calcined gypsum (plaster of Paris) are 2520.20.00. Both are Free under the general rate. Gypsum board, drywall and ceiling boards are heading 6809.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on graphite from China?
faqs.answer: Natural graphite from China (2504) pays 25% under Section 301 since January 1, 2026 (9903.91.06). It is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so graphite from other countries pays nothing extra and China does not pay the 12.5% on top. No antidumping or countervailing duty applies: the ITC voted against duties on active anode material from China on April 3, 2026. Synthetic graphite is chapter 38.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for graphite?
faqs.answer: Natural graphite is heading 2504: crystalline flake (not flake dust) 2504.10.10, other powder or flakes 2504.10.50 and other natural graphite 2504.90.00, all Free under the general rate. Artificial (synthetic) graphite is 3801.10, and graphite electrodes 8545.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on granite and marble?
faqs.answer: Blocks and slabs merely cut are in Chapter 25: granite 2.8%, travertine and sandstone 3%, marble Free. On top: Brazil 37.5% (40.3% in total on cut granite), Türkiye 12.5%, India 10%, Italy and Spain 10% in total, China 37.5% or more. Polished slabs, tiles and countertops are heading 6802, with different rates.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for granite, marble or natural stone?
faqs.answer: Crude or merely cut blocks and slabs: marble 2515.11 (crude) and 2515.12.10 (cut), travertine 2515.12.20, granite 2516.11 (crude) and 2516.12 (cut), sandstone 2516.20, other building stone 2516.90. Granules and powder of marble or granite are 2517.41 and 2517.49. Polished or otherwise worked stone, including countertops and tiles, is heading 6802.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sand, quartz, limestone or lime?
faqs.answer: Silica and quartz sand 2505.10, other natural sand 2505.90, quartz 2506.10, quartzite 2506.20; limestone flux and limestone for lime or cement 2521.00, crushed limestone for aggregate 2517.10; quicklime 2522.10, slaked (hydrated) lime 2522.20 and hydraulic lime 2522.30. All are Free under the general rate. Engineered quartz slabs and countertops are heading 6810.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sulfur?
faqs.answer: Sulfur of all kinds — crude, granular, prilled or molten — is 2503.00.00 (crude or unrefined 2503.00.00.10, other .90), Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. Sublimed, precipitated and colloidal sulfur are 2802.00.00.

faqs.question: Are building and construction materials affected by tariffs?
faqs.answer: For the Chapter 25 materials — cement, gypsum, lime, sand, gravel and building stone — yes, through the 2026 Section 301 tariffs: 12.5% for Türkiye, Vietnam and Egypt, 10% for the EU and India, nothing for USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico; China pays up to 37.5%. The IEEPA tariffs of 2025 ended February 24, 2026.
